topic: Research question: when an LLM generates text one token at a time, does the hidden representation used to produce token t already encode most of the MEANING of the sentence/thought being constructed, not just the identity of the next few tokens? Background you must engage with, not rediscover: (1) Future Lens (Pal et al., CoNLL 2023, arXiv:2311.04897) showed a single hidden state at GPT-J-6B token t linearly predicts exact token identities at positions >= t+2, with over 48% accuracy at some layers, via linear probing plus causal patching. (2) ESP / Efficient Training-Free Multi-Token Prediction (ICML 2026, arXiv:2603.17942) exploited the same latent multi-token-prediction property purely for speculative-decoding speedups, an engineering application, not a meaning/semantics study. Neither paper tests semantic content (recovering the MEANING of the eventual full continuation, not just literal next-token ids) or a long horizon (full sentence/clause) or a causal semantic-steering intervention. Design and run a first small-scale experiment testing this stronger semantic-level hypothesis, explicitly positioned as different from both prior papers: (a) use a small-to-medium open-weights causal LM such as GPT-2-large/xl or Pythia-1.4b/2.8b, pick one that fits and runs fast enough to iterate, only GPU 0 is available with about 98GB VRAM; (b) generate many short continuations from varied prompts; (c) take the hidden state at an early token position (e.g. right after the prompt) at a few candidate layers; (d) train a lightweight probe to predict a SENTENCE EMBEDDING of the full eventual continuation from that single early hidden state, evaluate with cosine similarity against the true continuation embedding compared to sensible baselines (random continuation, mean continuation embedding); (e) if a semantic probe direction is found, run a causal check by perturbing the hidden state along that direction and testing whether the resulting generations semantic embedding shifts in the predicted direction versus a random-direction control of the same magnitude; (f) report real numbers and explicitly discuss how this experiments evaluation (semantic recoverability plus causal semantic steering, long horizon) differs from Future Lens (token-identity probing, short horizon) and ESP (speculative decoding application), and state clearly whether the original hypothesis is supported, partially supported, or not supported by what was actually run. Keep the first cycle small enough to get a real result within the time budget; scale up in later cycles if time and cycle budget allow.
progress:
Cycle 1 review: ACCEPT - The experiment appears to have run successfully end-to-end, produced the required artifacts, and met the stated success criteria on the reported numbers. Criterion 1 is clearly satisfied: the best probe test cosine at layer 20 is 0.4283, which exceeds both the mean baseline (0.2310) by +0.1973 and the random-match baseline (0.0616) by a large margin, and even beats the optional lexical TF-IDF baseline (0.3612). Criterion 2 is also satisfied: retrieval Recall@5 is 0.759 versus random-chance 0.0602, a very large separation. Criterion 3 is satisfied on the reported steering metrics: the learned semantic direction shows the expected sign for +alpha and -alpha, exceeds the matched random-direction control, and crosses the >55% directional-shift threshold for both sentiment directions; the temporal contrast is even stronger. Criterion 4 is satisfied because the final verdict is explicitly reported as 'supported' and the writeup reportedly includes the requested contrast with Future Lens and ESP.

The only notable protocol deviations were (1) extending the ridge alpha grid beyond the initially suggested range and (2) retuning the steering alpha / refining the random-direction control after pilot results. These changes are reasonable, transparently documented, and do not look like execution mistakes. Extending alpha search is especially justified given the observed under-regularization in the original grid, and the steering pilot adjustment still preserves the core hypothesis test rather than invalidating it.

Because the experiment achieved the predeclared success conditions and there is no sign of an implementation failure that would warrant rerunning the same hypothesis, no further iteration is required for this cycle.
